name: Heat Index (NOAA)
description: Computes the heat index, or apparent temperature, from air temperature and relative humidity using the NOAA regression equation. It expresses how hot it feels when humidity slows the body's evaporative cooling.
notes: Temperature must be in Fahrenheit and humidity as a percent; the polynomial is only valid for hot, humid conditions above roughly 80°F. Assumes shade and light wind.

name: Wind Chill
description: Calculates the wind-chill temperature from air temperature and wind speed, expressing how cold the air feels as moving air strips heat from exposed skin. It uses the North American wind-chill formula in metric units.
notes: Temperature in Celsius and wind speed in km/h; valid only for temperatures at or below 10°C and winds above about 4.8 km/h. Applies to exposed skin, not sheltered areas.

name: Dew Point (Magnus)
description: Computes the dew point from air temperature and relative humidity using the Magnus formula. The dew point is the temperature to which air must be cooled at constant pressure for its water vapor to begin condensing.
notes: Temperature in Celsius and humidity as a percent. The Magnus coefficients are an approximation accurate to a few hundredths of a degree over normal atmospheric ranges.

name: Relative Humidity from Dew Point
description: Derives relative humidity from air temperature and dew point using the ratio of saturation vapor pressures at the two temperatures via the Magnus approximation. A dew point close to the air temperature yields humidity near 100 percent.
notes: Both temperatures in Celsius; dew point cannot exceed air temperature or humidity would exceed 100 percent. Result is a percent.

name: Saturation Vapor Pressure (Tetens)
description: Computes the saturation vapor pressure of water over a liquid surface at a given air temperature using the Tetens formula. This is the maximum partial pressure water vapor can exert before condensing at that temperature.
notes: Temperature in Celsius, result in hectopascals, valid for temperatures above 0°C over water. A different coefficient set applies for saturation over ice.

name: Barometric Altitude
description: Estimates altitude above sea level from measured air pressure and sea-level reference pressure using the international barometric formula. As pressure falls with height, the ratio of the two pressures maps to an altitude in meters.
notes: Both pressures in the same units (hPa). Assumes the standard atmosphere temperature profile, so real altitudes differ when actual conditions depart from standard.

name: Pressure at Altitude
description: Predicts air pressure at a given altitude from the sea-level pressure using the standard atmosphere model. Pressure decreases with height following a power law tied to the standard temperature lapse rate.
notes: Altitude in meters, pressure in hPa. Valid within the troposphere and assumes standard-atmosphere temperatures; it is the inverse of the barometric altitude formula.

name: Lapse-Rate Temperature
description: Computes air temperature at altitude by subtracting the lapse rate times the height gain from the surface temperature. It gives the expected cooling of air as one climbs at a constant rate of temperature decrease.
notes: Lapse rate is in °C per meter (the standard value is 0.0065); altitude in meters. Real atmospheres show inversions and varying lapse rates, so this is an idealization.

name: Richter Energy Release
description: Estimates the seismic energy radiated by an earthquake from its magnitude using the Gutenberg-Richter energy relation. Because it is exponential, each unit of magnitude corresponds to about 31.6 times more energy.
notes: Result is in joules and grows very rapidly, so small magnitude errors change energy greatly. The constants apply to the classic energy-magnitude relation, not moment magnitude directly.

name: Moment Magnitude
description: Converts the seismic moment of an earthquake into the moment magnitude scale using the standard logarithmic relation. Seismic moment measures the total energy released via fault area, slip, and rock rigidity.
notes: Seismic moment must be in newton-meters and uses base-10 logarithm. Moment magnitude is preferred over the Richter scale for large earthquakes because it does not saturate.

name: Earthquake Energy Ratio
description: Computes how many times more energy one earthquake releases than another from the difference in their magnitudes. It applies the rule that each magnitude unit corresponds to about 31.6 times more radiated energy.
notes: The result is a dimensionless multiple; a difference of 2 magnitudes gives roughly 1000 times the energy. Sign matters, since m1 minus m2 sets the direction of comparison.

name: Distance to Horizon
description: Estimates the straight-line distance to the visible horizon from the observer's eye height and the Earth's radius. It follows from geometry as the square root of twice the radius times the eye height.
notes: Eye height and radius in meters, result in meters; ignores atmospheric refraction, which typically extends the true horizon somewhat. Valid when eye height is small versus radius.

name: Great-Circle Distance
description: Computes the shortest surface distance between two points on a sphere from their latitudes and longitudes using the spherical law of cosines. Multiplying the central angle by the Earth's radius gives the great-circle distance.
notes: All coordinates in radians and radius in kilometers. The law of cosines loses precision for very short distances; the haversine formula is more numerically stable there.

name: Rainfall Volume
description: Calculates the total volume of water falling on a catchment by multiplying its horizontal area by the depth of rainfall. It gives the cubic meters of water collected over the surface.
notes: Rain depth must be in meters (convert from millimeters by dividing by 1000) and area in square meters. Assumes uniform rainfall and no losses to infiltration or evaporation.

name: Rational-Method Runoff
description: Estimates peak stormwater runoff using the rational method, multiplying a runoff coefficient, rainfall intensity, and drainage area. The factor 360 converts the mixed units into a peak discharge in cubic meters per second.
notes: Runoff coefficient is a fraction from 0 to 1, intensity in mm/h, area in hectares. Suited to small catchments; assumes steady rain lasting at least the time of concentration.

name: Slope Grade (Percent)
description: Expresses the steepness of a slope as a percent grade by dividing vertical rise by horizontal run and multiplying by 100. A 100 percent grade corresponds to a 45-degree slope where rise equals run.
notes: Rise and run must share the same length unit. Percent grade is not the same as the slope angle in degrees; the two coincide only near zero.

name: Slope Angle
description: Converts a slope's vertical rise and horizontal run into an inclination angle in degrees using the arctangent of their ratio. It gives the true angle the slope makes with the horizontal.
notes: Rise and run in the same length unit; the arctangent returns radians, which the factor 180 over pi converts to degrees. Angle stays below 90 degrees for any finite run.

name: Grade to Angle
description: Converts a percent grade into a slope angle in degrees by taking the arctangent of the grade divided by 100. It translates the road-sign style steepness figure into a geometric angle.
notes: Grade is entered as a percent, so 100 percent maps to 45 degrees. Output is in degrees; the relationship is nonlinear, so doubling the grade does not double the angle.

name: Wind Power Density
description: Computes the power carried by wind per unit area facing the flow, from air density and wind speed. Because it varies with the cube of speed, doubling the wind speed multiplies available power by eight.
notes: Air density in kg per cubic meter, speed in m/s, result in watts per square meter. This is the raw resource; a turbine extracts at most about 59 percent (the Betz limit).

name: Beaufort to Wind Speed
description: Converts a Beaufort scale number into an approximate wind speed in meters per second using the empirical power relation 0.836 times the Beaufort number to the three-halves power. It maps the descriptive scale to a physical speed.
notes: Beaufort number is dimensionless (0 to 12); the result is the mid-range speed for that force. It is an approximation, as each Beaufort force actually spans a range of speeds.

name: Tsunami Wave Speed
description: Calculates the speed of a shallow-water wave such as a tsunami as the square root of gravity times water depth. In deep ocean this gives the very high propagation speeds typical of tsunamis.
notes: Valid in the shallow-water regime where wavelength greatly exceeds depth, which holds for tsunamis even over deep oceans. Depth in meters, result in m/s.

name: Coriolis Parameter
description: Computes the Coriolis parameter from the Earth's angular velocity and latitude as twice the angular velocity times the sine of latitude. It quantifies the strength of the Coriolis effect that deflects moving air and water.
notes: Latitude in radians; the parameter is zero at the equator and maximal at the poles, and its sign is opposite between hemispheres. Angular velocity is Earth's rotation rate in rad/s.

name: UV Index (approx.)
description: Approximates the ultraviolet index by dividing the erythemal (sunburn-weighted) irradiance by 25 milliwatts per square meter, the value defined to equal one UV index unit. Higher values signal a greater risk of skin damage.
notes: Input must be erythemally weighted irradiance in mW per square meter, not raw UV power. The index is dimensionless and typically ranges from 0 to about 11 or more.

name: Solar Declination
description: Estimates the sun's declination angle for a given day of the year using a cosine-based approximation. Declination is the latitude at which the sun is directly overhead, swinging between about plus and minus 23.45 degrees over the year.
notes: Day of year is 1 to 365; the inner angle is converted to radians before the sine. It is an approximation ignoring orbital eccentricity, accurate to a fraction of a degree.

name: Day Length (approx.)
description: Estimates the number of daylight hours from the observer's latitude and the sun's declination. The sunrise hour angle is found from the two angles, then converted into hours of daylight.
notes: Latitude and declination in radians; the arccosine gives degrees via 180 over pi and the 2 over 15 factor turns degrees of hour angle into hours. Ignores refraction and fails within polar day or night.

name: Carbon Footprint (Travel)
description: Estimates the carbon dioxide emissions of a trip by multiplying distance traveled by an emission factor per kilometer. The factor reflects the emissions of the chosen mode of transport.
notes: Distance in kilometers and factor in kg CO2 per km; result is kilograms of CO2. Accuracy depends entirely on choosing an emission factor that matches the actual vehicle and occupancy.

name: River Discharge (Area-Velocity)
description: Computes river discharge, the volume of water passing per second, by multiplying the flow cross-sectional area by the average flow velocity. It is the basic area-velocity method of streamflow measurement.
notes: Area in square meters and velocity in m/s give discharge in cubic meters per second. Use the mean velocity across the section, since velocity varies with depth and position.

name: Sea-Level Pressure Reduction
description: Reduces a weather station's measured pressure to the equivalent sea-level pressure using station altitude and air temperature. This correction lets pressures from stations at different elevations be compared on weather maps.
notes: Station pressure in hPa, altitude in meters, temperature in Celsius (converted to kelvin inside). It assumes a standard lapse rate, so results are approximate in unusual conditions.

name: Vapor Pressure Deficit
description: Computes the vapor pressure deficit, the gap between the saturation vapor pressure at the air temperature and the actual vapor pressure. It measures the air's drying power, driving plant transpiration and evaporation.
notes: Temperature in Celsius and humidity as a percent; result in hectopascals. It uses the Tetens saturation formula, so it shares that formula's above-water, above-freezing validity.

name: Absolute Humidity
description: Computes absolute humidity, the actual mass of water vapor per cubic meter of air, from air temperature and relative humidity. It combines the saturation vapor pressure with the ideal gas law to weigh the water vapor present.
notes: Temperature in Celsius and humidity as a percent; result in grams per cubic meter. Unlike relative humidity, this gives a true concentration independent of temperature.

name: Mixing Ratio
description: Computes the mixing ratio, the mass of water vapor per kilogram of dry air, from the water vapor pressure and the total air pressure. The factor 621.97 comes from the ratio of the molar masses of water and dry air.
notes: Vapor pressure and total pressure in the same units (hPa); result in grams per kilogram. Vapor pressure must be below total pressure, and it divides by dry-air pressure (total minus vapor).

name: Potential Temperature
description: Computes potential temperature, the temperature a parcel of air would have if brought adiabatically to a reference pressure of 1000 hPa. It lets meteorologists compare the thermal state of air at different pressure levels.
notes: Temperature in kelvin and pressure in hPa; the exponent 0.286 is the ratio of the gas constant to the specific heat for dry air. Reference pressure is fixed at 1000 hPa.

name: Cloud Base Height (Espy)
description: Estimates the height of a cumulus cloud base above the surface from the spread between air temperature and dew point, using Espy's rule of about 125 meters per degree of spread. A drier surface (larger spread) implies a higher cloud base.
notes: Both temperatures in Celsius; the difference drives the result, so their absolute values do not matter. It is a rough rule of thumb for convective cumulus clouds only.

name: Celsius to Fahrenheit
description: Converts a temperature from degrees Celsius to degrees Fahrenheit by multiplying by nine-fifths and adding 32. This maps the freezing point of water at 0°C to 32°F and the boiling point at 100°C to 212°F.
notes: The additive constant 32 accounts for the different zero points of the two scales, so you cannot simply scale by 9/5 alone. The scales coincide at minus 40 degrees.

name: Fahrenheit to Celsius
description: Converts a temperature from degrees Fahrenheit to degrees Celsius by subtracting 32 and then multiplying by five-ninths. It is the inverse of the Celsius-to-Fahrenheit conversion.
notes: Subtract 32 before scaling, not after, since the scales have different zero points. The two scales read the same value at minus 40 degrees.

name: Wind Pressure
description: Estimates the dynamic pressure a wind exerts on a surface facing it, using the simplified relation 0.613 times wind speed squared. The coefficient bundles half the standard air density, so pressure rises with the square of speed.
notes: Wind speed in m/s, result in pascals. The 0.613 factor assumes standard sea-level air density; it gives stagnation pressure, before shape and gust factors used in structural codes.

name: Air Density (Ideal Gas)
description: Computes the density of dry air from pressure and absolute temperature using the ideal gas law with the specific gas constant for air (287.05 J per kg per kelvin). Density rises with pressure and falls as temperature increases.
notes: Pressure in pascals and temperature in kelvin, not Celsius. It treats air as dry; humid air is slightly less dense, which this formula does not account for.

name: Deep-Water Wave Speed
description: Gives the phase speed of a surface gravity wave in deep water as sqrt(g×L/(2π)), where L is the wavelength. Longer waves travel faster, so the speed grows with the square root of wavelength.
notes: Valid only in deep water, where depth exceeds about half the wavelength; in shallow water the speed depends on depth instead. Result is phase (crest) speed, not group speed.

name: Deep-Water Wavelength
description: Computes the wavelength of a deep-water surface wave from its period T using g×T²/(2π). The wavelength grows with the square of the period, so longer-period swells are much longer waves.
notes: Applies only to deep water where depth is more than about half the wavelength. Period must be in seconds; the dispersion relation breaks down in shallow or intermediate depths.

name: Manning Open-Channel Velocity
description: Manning's equation estimates the mean flow velocity in an open channel as (1/n)×R^(2/3)×S^(1/2), from roughness n, hydraulic radius R, and slope S. Rougher channels or gentler slopes give slower flow.
notes: This SI form has no unit conversion factor; use R in metres and S as a dimensionless slope. Assumes steady, uniform, turbulent flow; n is empirical and varies with channel lining.

name: Darcy Groundwater Velocity
description: Darcy's law gives the groundwater Darcy flux (specific discharge) as hydraulic conductivity K times hydraulic gradient i. It is the volumetric flow per unit total cross-sectional area of the aquifer.
notes: This is the Darcy velocity, not the actual pore velocity; divide by porosity to get seepage velocity. Valid for slow, laminar flow through saturated porous media.

name: Torricelli Outflow Velocity
description: Torricelli's theorem gives the ideal efflux speed of liquid leaving an opening under a head h as sqrt(2×g×h). It equals the speed a body would reach falling freely from that height.
notes: Ignores viscosity and contraction; a real orifice needs a discharge coefficient below 1. Head h is the vertical distance from the free surface down to the opening.

name: Solar Elevation Angle
description: Computes the sun's elevation angle above the horizon in degrees from latitude, solar declination, and hour angle, using the standard spherical-astronomy relation. Higher values mean the sun is nearer the zenith.
notes: All three inputs must be in radians; the result is converted to degrees. Ignores atmospheric refraction; negative values mean the sun is below the horizon.

name: Kelvin to Celsius
description: Converts an absolute temperature in kelvin to degrees Celsius by subtracting 273.15. The two scales share the same size of degree, so only the zero point shifts.
notes: Use 273.15 exactly, not 273. A negative result simply means a temperature below the freezing point of water; kelvin inputs cannot be negative.

name: Snow Water Equivalent
description: Gives the snow water equivalent, the depth of water produced if the snowpack melted, as snow depth times the ratio of snow density to water density (1000 kg/m³). Denser snow yields more water.
notes: Depth and result share the same length unit here (mm); density must be in kg/m³. Assumes water density of 1000 kg/m³ and a uniform snowpack.

name: Beaufort from Wind Speed
description: Estimates the Beaufort wind-force number from wind speed v using the empirical relation (v/0.836)^(2/3). It converts a measured speed in m/s into the traditional 0–12 force scale.
notes: Wind speed must be in m/s; the raw result is fractional and normally rounded to the nearest whole force number. The scale is empirical and caps at force 12.

name: Epicenter Distance from S-P Interval (Omori's Formula)
description: Estimates the distance from a seismograph station to an earthquake epicenter using Omori's formula, k*(ts-tp), from the S-P arrival time interval. The larger the delay between P- and S-wave arrivals, the farther the epicenter.
notes: The constant k depends on local crustal velocity structure and is commonly taken near 8 km/s, though regional values vary from about 7 to 9. ts and tp must be in seconds.
